metadata.title: Decoding divides: The role of socioeconomic status and personality traits in AI divides and educational inequality

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a regional survey (Education Monitor Limburg) linked to national registry data for Grade 6 students in the Netherlands (2022–2023). The analytic sample is restricted to participating schools and then further restricted to students with complete data on the three personality traits, AI usage intensity, digital literacy, and family SES (final N=4,497). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the mediation models are estimated with OLS using robust standard errors clustered at the school level. Because no explicit sampling-weight variable is documented, results should be interpreted as conditional on the participating-school sample rather than as fully design-weighted population estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were drawn from the 2022–2023 wave of the Education Monitor Limburg (OML) targeting Grade 6 students in Limburg province. The initial sample comprised 6,772 students (~75% of Grade 6 students in the province) before exclusions. The final analytic sample (N=4,497) includes only students with complete data on the three personality traits (openness, extraversion, perseverance), AI usage intensity, digital literacy, and family SES; missingness was handled via listwise deletion. The authors note that most missing observations likely reflect entire non-participating schools rather than item-level skipping, and they therefore did not conduct a formal selectivity analysis of responding vs non-responding institutions.

main_findings.dataset_used: OML 2022–2023 Netherlands Grade 6 academic performance (exit test score percentiles)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Parallel mediation (PROCESS Model 4, OLS with school-cluster robust SEs; indirect effects via 5,000 bootstrap samples). Digital literacy → performance: B=1.78, SE=0.37, 95% CI [1.06, 2.51]. SES direct effect on performance: B=0.23, SE=0.02, 95% CI [0.18, 0.27]. AI usage intensity showed no significant mediation paths (e.g., SES → AI usage → performance: indirect B≈−0.0000, 95% CI [−0.0006, 0.0006]; AI usage → performance path: B=0.029, SE=0.66, 95% CI [−1.27, 1.33]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using OML 2022–2023 Netherlands Grade 6 academic performance (exit test score percentiles) the study leveraged digital literacy, family SES, and personality traits (openness, extraversion, perseverance) to model academic performance via parallel mediation with AI usage intensity and digital literacy, finding that digital literacy significantly (and partially) mediated personality–performance relationships while AI usage intensity did not mediate any of the personality–performance links. This indicates that in AI-integrated classrooms, educational inequality is more strongly tied to students’ digital skills than to whether they use AI tools, implying that policy should prioritize skill-building and differentiated digital literacy support rather than access alone.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes mediation pathways linking family SES and personality traits (openness, extraversion, perseverance) to Grade 6 academic performance in the Netherlands using Education Monitor Limburg (OML) 2022–2023 data linked to national registry exit test scores (final analytic sample N=4,497). Academic performance was operationalized as within-test-provider national percentiles to align heterogeneous test scales, and the two mediators were AI usage intensity and digital literacy. AI usage intensity was constructed using a CatBoost model that predicts students’ self-reported digital tool usage frequency from teacher-reported tool-context indicators, while digital literacy and personality traits were scaled using GRM-based IRT composites. In parallel mediation (PROCESS Model 4), digital literacy showed a significant positive association with performance (B=1.78, SE=0.37, 95% CI [1.06, 2.51]) and produced significant indirect effects for all three personality traits, whereas AI usage intensity showed no significant mediation. The study uses OLS with school-cluster robust SEs and listwise deletion for missingness; it is cross-sectional, so mediation is correlational rather than causal.
